messages.content: You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does "Reveal" mean in Magic: The Gathering?
To show a card to all players for a brief time. See rule 701.20, “Reveal.”
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What happens when an effect attempts to end the combat phase outside of a combat phase according to rule 724.2g?
Nothing happens. Rule 724.2g states that if an effect attempts to end the combat phase at any time that’s not a combat phase, nothing happens.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does "Max Speed" mean in Magic: The Gathering?

1. A player has max speed if their speed is 4. See rule 702.179, “Start Your Engines!” 2. A keyword ability that grants an ability to the permanent or card it’s on only if that permanent’s controller (or that card’s owner, if it isn’t on the battlefield) has a speed of 4. See rule 702.178, “Max Speed.”
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What are the subtypes for enchantments, lands, and planeswalkers?

Enchantments have subtypes such as Aura, Background, Cartouche, Case, Class, Curse, Plan, Role, Room, Rune, Saga, and Shrine (205.3h, 205.3i, 205.3j). Lands have subtypes like Cave, Desert, Forest, Gate, Island, Lair, Locus, Mine, Mountain, Plains, Planet, Power-Plant, Sphere, Swamp, Tower, Town, and Urza’s, with Forest, Island, Mountain, Plains, and Swamp being the basic land types (205.3i). Planeswalkers have subtypes such as Ajani, Aminatou, Angrath, and so on (205.3j).
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What is the role of the starting player in the game?
The starting player is considered the active player and each other player is considered a nonactive player. This is stated in rule 101.4e.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What are the characteristics of a face-down permanent on the battlefield?

A face-down permanent on the battlefield has no characteristics other than being a 2/2 face-down creature with no text, no name, no subtypes, and no mana cost, unless otherwise specified by the effect that put it onto the battlefield face down or allowed it to be cast face down. (708.2a)
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does "Archenemy Commander" mean in Magic: The Gathering?
A Commander game that follows a modified version of the Archenemy rules. See rule 903, “Commander,” and rule 904, “Archenemy.”
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What happens when a player chooses to put their commander into the command zone using the replacement effect described in rule 903.9b?

The permanent and each component representing it that isn’t a commander are put into the appropriate zone, and the card that represents it and is a commander is put into the command zone. (See rules 903.9b and 903.9c)
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What is a dungeon card and how is it brought into the game?

A dungeon card is a card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards. It begins outside the game and is brought into the game using the venture into the dungeon keyword action. See rules 309.1 and 309.2.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What is the role of an emperor in the Emperor variant of Magic: The Gathering?

The emperor is the middle player on each team in an Emperor game. The emperor cannot attack any opponents, even if the generals are within their spell range. The range of influence for an emperor is limited to 2. (See rules 809.2, 809.3a, and 809.3b)
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does "Firebending" mean in Magic: The Gathering?
A keyword ability that adds red mana until end of combat whenever a creature with that ability attacks. See rule 702.189, “Firebending.”
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does "Meld" mean in Magic: The Gathering?
To turn two members of a meld pair so their back faces are up and combined into one oversized Magic card. See rule 701.42, “Meld.”
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does "Attack" mean in Magic: The Gathering?
To send a creature into combat offensively. A creature can attack a player or a planeswalker. See rule 508, “Declare Attackers Step.”
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What happens when a creature spell resolves?
When a creature spell resolves, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control. (302.2)
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does "Undaunted" mean in Magic: The Gathering?
A keyword ability that reduces the cost of a spell based on the number of opponents you have. See rule 702.125, “Undaunted.”
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does the rule say about the restrictions and additional effects of mana produced by spells or abilities that create multiple mana types?

Some spells or abilities that produce mana can have restrictions or additional effects that apply to all mana produced. If the spell or ability creates a delayed triggered ability that triggers when the mana is spent, a separate delayed triggered ability is created for each mana produced. If the spell or ability creates a continuous effect or replacement effect if the mana is spent, a separate effect is created once for each mana produced. (See rules 106.6a)
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does "Proliferate" mean in Magic: The Gathering?
To give an additional counter to any number of players and/or permanents of each kind they already have. See rule 701.34, “Proliferate.”
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does "Mutate" mean in Magic: The Gathering?
A keyword that lets a creature card be cast as a mutating creature spell. See rule 702.140, “Mutate.”
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What is a scheme card and how does it function in the game?

A scheme card is a nontraditional card type used in the Archenemy casual variant. It remains in the command zone and has no subtypes. Its static, triggered, and activated abilities affect the game as long as it is face up. Scheme cards are not permanents and can’t be cast. If a non-ongoing scheme card is face up and no triggered abilities are on the stack, it is turned face down and put on the bottom of its owner’s scheme deck. (See rules 314.2, 314.3, 314.4, and 314.6.)
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What is a kindred card and how does it function in the game?

A kindred card is a card that has another card type and follows the rules for casting and resolving a card of that other card type. Kindred subtypes are usually a single word long and are listed after a long dash, such as 'Kindred Enchantment — Merfolk.' These subtypes are part of the set of creature types. See rules 308.1 and 308.2 for more details.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What is an additional cost in Magic: The Gathering?

An additional cost is a cost listed in a spell’s rules text or applied to a spell or ability from another effect, that its controller must pay at the same time they pay the spell’s mana cost or the ability’s activation cost. See rule 118.8 and rule 601.2b for more details.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What happens if a calculation yields a negative number for a creature's power or toughness?

If a calculation yields a negative number for a creature's power or toughness, zero is used instead, unless that effect doubles, triples, or sets to a specific value a player’s life total or the power and/or toughness of a creature or creature card. (See rule 107.1b)
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What is the value of X when a spell or activated ability has an {X} in its cost and the value is not defined by the text of the spell or ability?
The value of X is chosen by the controller of the spell or ability as part of casting the spell or activating the ability. (See rule 107.3a)
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What happens if a player on a team in Two-Headed Giant loses the game?
The team loses the game. (810.8a)
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does "Double" mean in Magic: The Gathering?
A keyword action used in a variety of contexts. See rule 701.10, “Double.”
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What is a special action in Magic: The Gathering?

A special action is an action a player may take when they have priority that doesn’t use the stack. Special actions include playing a land, turning a face-down creature face up, ignoring the effect of a static ability, discarding a card, exiling a card with suspend, and putting a companion card from outside the game into your hand. These actions can be taken at specific times when a player has priority, as detailed in rules 116.2a through 116.2g.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does "Cipher" mean in Magic: The Gathering?
A keyword ability that allows you to encode a card on a creature and cast that card whenever that creature deals combat damage to a player. See rule 702.99, “Cipher.”
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does "Cumulative Upkeep" mean in Magic: The Gathering?
A keyword ability that imposes an increasing cost to keep a permanent on the battlefield. See rule 702.24, “Cumulative Upkeep.”
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What happens if a player gains 0 life in a life gain event?

If a player gains 0 life, no life gain event has occurred, and abilities triggered by life gain won’t trigger, and replacement effects that would replace a life gain event won’t apply. This is because the rules treat gaining 0 life as no life gain event, and they are written to only trigger or apply when a life gain event actually occurs. (See rules 119.9 and 119.10)
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does "Permanent" mean in Magic: The Gathering?
A card or token on the battlefield. See rule 110, “Permanents.”
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does the term 'ability' refer to in the context of Magic: The Gathering?

In the context of Magic: The Gathering, an ability is text on an object that explains what that object does or can do, or an activated or triggered ability on the stack. This kind of ability is an object. See rule 113, “Abilities,” and section 6, “Spells, Abilities, and Effects.”
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What happens when a Siege battle's defense is 0 and it isn't the source of an ability which has triggered but not yet left the stack?
The Siege battle is put into its owner's graveyard. (See rule 310.7)
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does a player commit a crime when doing in Magic: The Gathering?

A player commits a crime when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or put a triggered ability on the stack and that spell or ability targets at least one opponent; at least one permanent, spell, or ability an opponent controls; and/or at least one card in an opponent’s graveyard. (Rule 700.13)
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What happens if an effect copies a spell with multiple targets and the target is no longer legal when the copy resolves?

The copy isn’t created. If the spell or ability has more than one target, each of the copy’s targets must be that player or object. If that player or object isn’t a legal target for each instance of the word ‘target,’ the copy isn’t created. (See rule 707.10e)
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does "Dredge" mean in Magic: The Gathering?
A keyword ability that lets a player return a card from their graveyard to their hand. See rule 702.52, “Dredge.”
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What are the five colors of mana in Magic: The Gathering?
The five colors of mana in Magic: The Gathering are white, blue, black, red, and green (106.1a).
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What is the process for determining excess damage to a permanent after it has been dealt damage by multiple sources?

The process for determining excess damage to a permanent after it has been dealt damage by multiple sources is as follows: First, the total damage dealt by the sources is compared to the lethal damage for creatures, the loyalty of planeswalkers, or the defense of battles. If the total damage exceeds the relevant threshold, the excess damage is calculated as the difference. This excess damage is then dealt to the permanent. The specific rule that describes this process is 120.10.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does "Zone-Change Triggers" mean in Magic: The Gathering?
Trigger events that involve objects changing zones. See rule 603.6.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
When does the active player get priority during the upkeep step?

The active player gets priority during the upkeep step after any abilities that triggered during the untap step and at the beginning of the upkeep are put onto the stack. This is stated in rule 503.1.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
When does the active player get priority after blockers are declared in a combat phase?
The active player gets priority after blockers are declared in a combat phase. This is stated in rule 509.2: 'Second, the active player gets priority.'
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
Player A draws a card, then Player B gets priority — what happens, and why?

Player B gets priority because after the active player (Player A) draws a card, the next step is for the active player to get priority. This is stated in rule 504.2, which says, 'Second, the active player gets priority.'
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
Where does an instant or sorcery card go if it would normally enter the battlefield, according to the rules text provided?
An instant or sorcery card remains in its previous zone if it would enter the battlefield, as stated in rule 400.4a.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
Where does a spell go when it is cast, and what triggers this action?
When a spell is cast, the physical card is put on the stack (505.1). This action is triggered by the player moving the card from where it is to the stack (601.2a).
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What is the sequence of steps a player must follow when declaring attackers, and what rules govern each step?

First, the active player checks each creature they control to see if it’s affected by any requirements (508.1d). Then, if any creatures have banding or a ‘bands with other’ ability, the active player announces which creatures, if any, are banded with which (508.1e). Next, the active player taps the chosen creatures (508.1f). If there are any optional costs to attack, the player chooses which, if any, they will pay (508.1g). The total cost to attack is then determined, which becomes locked in (508.1h). If any of the costs require mana, the player has a chance to activate mana abilities (508.1i). Finally, the player pays all costs in any order, ensuring they have enough mana in their pool (508.1j).
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
Player A casts a spell that reads 'When you have no cards in hand, draw a card.' Then Player B loses the game. What happens, and why?

The ability will not trigger because Player B losing the game does not match the condition of having no cards in hand. Rule 603.8 states that these abilities trigger when a game state is true, not when an event occurs. Player B losing the game is not an event that causes the hand to be empty, so the ability does not trigger. The specific rule reference is 603.8.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.

Player A casts a spell that reads 'When this spell resolves, put a +1/+1 counter on target creature', creating a delayed triggered ability. Player B taps the targeted creature before the spell resolves. What happens?

The delayed triggered ability will trigger when the targeted creature untaps, as it refers to the creature's characteristics at the time the ability resolves. The answer is based on rule 603.7c, which states that a delayed triggered ability that refers to a particular object still affects it even if the object changes characteristics.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.

Player A plays Ashiok, Wicked Manipulator and chooses to exile 2 cards from their library. Then, Player B plays Breeding Pool, a land that enters the battlefield and lets Player B pay 2 life. What happens, and why?

Ashiok's replacement effect will ignore Breeding Pool because it is entering the battlefield, and the next two cards will be exiled. This is because Ashiok's ability is a replacement effect that modifies how a permanent enters the battlefield, and another replacement effect (Breeding Pool's ability) causes a player to exile cards. Rule 614.13c states that any card that is entering the battlefield from that library won’t be included in that effect, even though those cards are in the library as the effect is applied.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
Player A casts a spell that creates a token, which has the ability to gain life. Player B has a card with the ability to replace the gain of life with drawing a card. What happens, and why?

Player B’s ability to replace the gain of life with drawing a card must be applied first (616.1g). After that, Player A’s ability on the token to gain life can be applied. The order of effects is important because the second effect can’t be chosen until after the first effect has been chosen (616.1g).
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
Player A casts Daunting Defender on a Cleric creature, then Player B casts Pyroclasm. What happens, and why?

Daunting Defender prevents 1 damage from Pyroclasm to the Cleric creature because the ability specifies 'If a source would deal damage to a Cleric creature you control, prevent 1 of that damage.' Pyroclasm deals 2 damage to each creature, so it will deal 1 damage to the Cleric creature controlled by Player A, as the ability only prevents 1 damage. Rule 615.10 explains the specific amount of damage that is prevented by the ability, and Rule 609.7b confirms that the damage is prevented based on the source's properties matching the ability's conditions.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
Player A casts a spell that reads 'All creatures get +1/+1 until end of turn', Player B responds by attacking with a creature — what happens?

Player B’s creature gets +1/+1 because the continuous effect from the spell modifies the characteristics of the creature. The effect is determined when the spell resolves, so it applies to the creature even if it wasn’t on the battlefield when the spell was cast. This follows rule 611.2c, which states that effects that modify characteristics are determined when the spell or ability resolves.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.

Player A casts a spell that causes a permanent to enter the battlefield with an ability marked with the anchor word 'Choose'. Then, Player B casts a spell that causes the same permanent to enter the battlefield with a different ability marked with the anchor word 'Choose'. What happens, and why?

Player B's spell will override Player A's spell because the second 'Choose' ability to enter the battlefield takes precedence. According to rule 614.12b, if multiple replacement effects that require choices from a player would modify how multiple permanents enter the battlefield simultaneously, that player may not make choices for those effects that would cause the combined costs of those effects to not be payable. Since both abilities are marked with 'Choose', the second choice takes precedence, and the permanent will enter the battlefield with the ability specified by Player B's spell. The answer is based on rule 614.12b.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.

Player A plays a creature with the ability 'When [this creature] enters the battlefield, put a +1/+1 counter on target creature.' Then Player B plays a creature with the ability 'Whenever a creature with a +1/+1 counter on it enters the battlefield, this creature gets +1/+1.' What happens, and why?

The second ability refers only to a creature put onto the battlefield as a result of the first ability. This is because the abilities are linked, as per rule 607.2g. The second ability will give the player's creature +1/+1, because the first ability caused a +1/+1 counter to be put on a creature, which is the trigger for the second ability.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.

Player A casts a spell that causes Player B to skip their draw step and instead tap all their artifacts. Then Player B plays a card that replaces the draw with an additional action. What happens, and why?

Player B skips their draw step and instead taps all their artifacts. Then, because of the card played by Player B, Player B performs the additional action but does not draw a card. This is because the replacement effect from Player B’s card is applied, and the additional action is performed as specified in rule 614.11a, which states that all actions required by the replacement are completed before resuming the sequence.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
Player A has a card in their hand that has the text 'You may cast this card only from your hand.', then Player B casts a spell that allows Player A to look at their hand. What happens, and why?

Player A can still only cast the card from their hand because the static ability on the card specifies that it can only be cast from the hand. Rule 604.6 states that such static abilities apply while a card is in any zone that you could cast or play it from, but it does not change the fact that the card can only be cast from the hand. Therefore, Player A can look at their hand but cannot cast the card from anywhere else. 604.6, 601.4
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
Player A plays a spell with the ability 'splice X onto [spell]' and then Player B applies a name sticker to the spell. What happens, and why?

The spell will have the rules text of the card with splice added to its ability, but the name of the spell will be changed to the word on the name sticker. This is because the splice ability adds the rules text of the card with splice to the spell, and the name sticker changes the name of the spell. The relevant rules are 612.10 and 123.6.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
Player A casts an Aura that gives a creature flying, then Player B casts an Aura that removes flying from the same creature. What happens, and why?

The effect that removes flying from the creature wins. According to rule 613.9, one continuous effect can override another. Since the effect from Player B’s Aura is applied after Player A’s, it overrides the flying granted by Player A’s Aura. The result is that the creature loses flying because the effect in timestamp order 'wins.'
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.

Player A controls a 2/2 creature. Player B activates a spell that gives the creature +1/+1, then Player A activates a spell that switches the creature’s power and toughness. What is the creature’s power and toughness now, and why?

The creature’s power and toughness is now 3/1. First, the +1/+1 effect from Player B’s spell is applied, making the creature a 3/3. Then, Player A’s spell switches the creature’s power and toughness, resulting in 3/1. Rule 613.4b applies the +1/+1 effect, and Rule 613.4d applies the switch effect, overriding the timestamp order because they are in the same sublayer.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.

Player A casts a spell that gives their creature +10/+10 and flying, then Player B responds by equipping an Aura that grants the same creature +10/+10 and flying. What is the order of the effects, and why?

The order of the effects is determined by their timestamps. The Aura's effect is applied after the spell's effect because the Aura is attached to the creature, and the timestamp of the Aura effect is later than the timestamp of the spell effect. This is because the Aura effect has the same timestamp as the Aura itself, which is created after the spell effect is applied. The rule 613.7a explains that a continuous effect generated by a static ability (like the Aura) has the same timestamp as the object the static ability is on, or the timestamp of the effect that created the ability, which in this case is Player A's spell.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does the evoke keyword ability allow a player to do when casting a spell, and what happens when the spell enters the battlefield with its evoke cost paid?

The evoke keyword ability allows a player to cast a card by paying its evoke cost rather than its mana cost. When the permanent enters the battlefield and its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it. This is described in rules 702.74a and 509.1a.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What happens to a permanent when it phases out according to the rules?

When a permanent phases out, its status changes to 'phased out.' It is treated as though it does not exist, can't affect or be affected by anything else in the game, and is removed from combat. This is described in rules 702.26b and 506.4.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What happens when a player controls a permanent with nightbound and it's day?

Any time a player controls a permanent that is back face up with nightbound and it’s day, that player transforms that permanent. This happens immediately and isn’t a state-based action. (Rule 702.145f)
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does the ability 'Mentor' do in Magic: The Gathering?
'Mentor' is a triggered ability that puts a +1/+1 counter on a target attacking creature with power less than the mentor creature's power whenever the mentor creature attacks. See rule 702.134a.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does the emerge keyword ability allow a player to do when casting a spell, and how does it reduce the spell's total cost?

The emerge keyword ability allows a player to cast a spell by paying a specified cost and sacrificing a creature, rather than paying the spell's mana cost. The total cost is reduced by an amount of generic mana equal to the sacrificed creature's mana value. This is described in rules 702.119a and 702.119b.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does the spree ability mean mechanically in terms of casting a spell with this ability?
The spree ability means 'Choose one or more modes. As an additional cost to cast this spell, pay the costs associated with those modes.' (Rule 702.172a)
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does the Battle Cry keyword ability do in combat?
The Battle Cry keyword ability makes other attacking creatures better in combat. See rule 702.91, 'Battle Cry'.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What happens if an effect instructs a player to meld objects that can't be melded?
The objects stay in their current zone. This is because rule 701.42c states that if an effect instructs a player to meld objects that can’t be melded, they stay in their current zone.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does the keyword ability 'Devour' do and how many +1/+1 counters are added to the permanent when it enters the battlefield?

Devour is a variant of devour. When an object with devour enters the battlefield, you may sacrifice any number of quality permanents. This permanent enters with N +1/+1 counters on it for each permanent sacrificed this way. The specific rule is 702.82c.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
What does the keyword action 'populate' do mechanically?
To populate means to choose a creature token you control and create a token that’s a copy of that creature token. (Rule 701.36a)
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.

Player A controls a permanent with start your engines! and has no speed, then Player B controls a permanent with a Role that has a timestamp, and Player A attaches the Role to the permanent with start your engines! — what happens, and why?

Player A’s speed becomes 1 because the Role with the start your engines! has the most recent timestamp. Rule 704.5z states that if a permanent has more than one Role attached, each of those Roles except the one with the most recent timestamp is put into its owner’s graveyard. Since Player A’s Role has the most recent timestamp, it remains on the permanent, and Player B’s Role is put into Player B’s graveyard. Rule 704.5aa specifies that if a player controls a permanent with start your engines! and that player has no speed, that player’s speed becomes 1.
You are a Magic: The Gathering rules expert. Answer precisely and cite comprehensive rule numbers.
Player A has 1 life and casts a spell that deals 2 damage to Player A. Then Player B has priority. What happens, and why?
Player B gets priority, and then a state-based action is checked. Since Player A now has 0 life, rule 704.5a triggers, and Player A loses the game. The answer is based on rule 704.5a.
